```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

Run the chunks in order. This notebook primarily uses a raw 10x Genomics count
matrices in the shared directory and - optionally - the corresponding filtered
matrix in a bonus exercise; update the paths if your data are elsewhere.
Rows represent genes and columns represent droplet barcodes. A unique molecular
identifier (UMI) labels an individual captured RNA molecule.

Load the packages used in this analysis:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(DropletUtils)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)
library(scDblFinder)
library(Seurat)
library(DoubletFinder)
library(celda)
library(scater)
library(scran)
library(sessioninfo)
```

# Empty droplets

See the [DropletUtils tutorial](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DropletUtils/inst/doc/DropletUtils.html)
for details of barcode handling and cell calling.

- Import the raw matrix into R; use `DropletUtils::read10xCounts()`.
  Make a `SingleCellExperiment` object called `sce`.

**Hint:**

- Use a named character vector for `samples`: the value is the data directory,
  and the name is a short sample label (for example, `pbmc5k`).
- Set `col.names = TRUE` to use barcodes as column names.
  This is key for a bonus exercise comparing your own filtering to
  CellRanger's own filtered matrix.

```{r}
library(DropletUtils)
sce <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts(
    samples = c("pbmc5k" = "/project/shared/.../raw_feature_bc_matrix"),
    col.names = TRUE
)
sce
```

- Remove barcodes with zero total counts to reduce computation.
  Empty droplets can still contain ambient RNA, so non-zero counts do not prove
  that a droplet contains a cell.

**Hint:** Use `colSums()` on the `"counts"` assay, then subset columns with a
total UMI count greater than zero.

```{r}
sce <- sce[, colSums(assay(sce, "counts")) > 0]
sce
```

- Run `DropletUtils::emptyDrops()` on the remaining droplets.

**Hint:** Use `set.seed()` to make randomised steps reproducible.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
out <- DropletUtils::emptyDrops(   )
out
```

**How do you read the output? Which droplets would you retain as cells?**

> Answer:
>
> The output is a table with one row per barcode.
>
> - `Total`: total UMI count.
> - `PValue`: small values provide evidence against ambient RNA alone.
> - `FDR`: p-value adjusted to control the false discovery rate across barcodes.
>
> Retain droplets with `FDR <= 0.01` as likely cell-containing droplets. This targets
> a false discovery rate of 1% among retained droplets; it is not the probability
> that an individual droplet is empty. Barcodes with `NA` FDR values are
> low-count droplets that were not tested. A high FDR does not prove a droplet is empty.

- Keep droplets called as cells and name the object `sce_filtered_emptydrops`.

**Hint:** Use `which(out$FDR <= 0.01)` to select matching columns. `which()`
returns indices for `TRUE` values and excludes `NA` values.

```{r}
sce_filtered_emptydrops <- sce[   ,  ]
sce_filtered_emptydrops
```

## Bonus

- Compare droplets called as cells, droplets not called as "non-cempty" droplets, and untested
  droplets using total UMI counts, mitochondrial percentages, and principal
  component analysis (PCA) coordinates.

**Note:** The `MT-` prefix matches human mitochondrial gene symbols. Other
annotations may differ. These plots are diagnostic; they do not replace cell calling.

```{r}
droplet_status <- case_when(
    is.na(out$FDR) ~ "Not tested",
    out$FDR <= 0.01 ~ "Called as cell",
    TRUE ~ "Not called as cell"
)
```

```{r}
plot_data <- tibble(
    library_size = colSums(assay(sce, "counts")),
    droplet_status = droplet_status
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(droplet_status, library_size)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) +
    scale_y_continuous(trans = "log10") +
    labs(x = "Droplet classification", y = "Total UMI count") +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
```

```{r}
is.mt <- grepl("^MT-", rowData(sce)[["Symbol"]])
plot_data <- tibble(
    total = colSums(assay(sce, "counts")),
    MT_total = colSums(assay(sce, "counts")[is.mt, ]),
    MT_percent = MT_total / total * 100,
    droplet_status = droplet_status
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(droplet_status, MT_percent)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) +
    labs(x = "Droplet classification", y = "Mitochondrial counts (%)") +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
```

```{r}
set.seed(1)
sce <- logNormCounts(sce)
sce <- runPCA(sce)
plot_data <- tibble(
    reducedDim(sce, "PCA")[, c("PC1", "PC2")] %>% as_tibble(),
    droplet_status = droplet_status
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(PC1, PC2, color = droplet_status)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(color = "Droplet classification") +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
```

- Import the Cell Ranger filtered matrix from the same sample and compare the
  retained barcodes with your emptyDrops calls. The methods may retain different cells.

```{r}
sce_filtered_cellranger <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts(
    samples = c("pbmc5k" = "/project/shared/.../filtered_feature_bc_matrix"),
    col.names = TRUE
)
all_barcodes <- colnames(sce) # use the 'larger' dataset that also contains empty droplets
compare_table <- tibble(
    emptydrops = all_barcodes %in% colnames(sce_filtered_emptydrops), # kept by your emptyDrops
    cellranger = all_barcodes %in% colnames(sce_filtered_cellranger), # kept by Cellranger
)
table(compare_table)
```

# Doublets

A doublet is a droplet containing two cells; a singlet contains one cell.
Continue with `sce_filtered_emptydrops`, which contains the droplets called as cells.
See the [scDblFinder tutorial](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/scDblFinder/inst/doc/scDblFinder.html)
for details of doublet detection.

- Run `scDblFinder::scDblFinder()`.
  Store the output in a new object called `sce_scdblfinder`.

**Hint:** Use `set.seed()` to make randomised steps reproducible.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
sce_scdblfinder <- scDblFinder(   )
```

- Use `table()` to count predicted doublets and singlets.

**Hint:** Predictions are stored in `colData(sce_scdblfinder)$scDblFinder.class`.

```{r}
table(   )
```

**How do you read the output? Which droplets would you consider doublets?**

> Answer:
>
> `scDblFinder()` returns a `SingleCellExperiment` with predictions in the cell
> metadata. `table()` counts each predicted class. Treat droplets labelled
> `"doublet"` in `scDblFinder.class` as predicted doublets.

- Remove doublets from the dataset.
  Call the new object `sce_filtered_scdblfinder`.

**Hint:** Keep columns labelled `"singlet"` in `scDblFinder.class`.

```{r}
sce_filtered_scdblfinder <- sce_scdblfinder[,   ]
sce_filtered_scdblfinder
```

## Bonus

- Compare predicted doublets and singlets using total UMI counts, mitochondrial
  percentages, and PCA coordinates.

```{r}
plot_data <- tibble(
    library_size = colSums(assay(sce_scdblfinder, "counts")),
    scdblfinder = sce_scdblfinder$scDblFinder.class
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(scdblfinder, library_size)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) +
    scale_y_continuous(trans = "log10") +
    labs(x = "Predicted class", y = "Total UMI count") +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
```

```{r}
is.mt <- grepl("^MT-", rowData(sce_scdblfinder)[["Symbol"]])
plot_data <- tibble(
    total = colSums(assay(sce_scdblfinder, "counts")),
    MT_total = colSums(assay(sce_scdblfinder, "counts")[is.mt, ]),
    MT_percent = MT_total / total * 100,
    scdblfinder = sce_scdblfinder$scDblFinder.class
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(scdblfinder, MT_percent)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) +
    labs(x = "Predicted class", y = "Mitochondrial counts (%)") +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
```

```{r}
set.seed(1)
sce_scdblfinder <- logNormCounts(sce_scdblfinder)
sce_scdblfinder <- runPCA(sce_scdblfinder)
plot_data <- tibble(
    reducedDim(sce_scdblfinder, "PCA")[, c("PC1", "PC2")] %>% as_tibble(),
    scdblfinder = sce_scdblfinder$scDblFinder.class
) %>%
    arrange(scdblfinder)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(PC1, PC2, color = scdblfinder)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(color = "Predicted class") +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
```

## Bonus: compare doublet detection methods

- Compare scDblFinder with [DoubletFinder](https://github.com/chris-mcginnis-ucsf/DoubletFinder).
  Start by creating and preprocessing a `Seurat` object.

**Note:** Chunks marked `eval=FALSE` are displayed but skipped during rendering.
Run them interactively in order to complete the comparison. The doublet rate
and `pK` below are example values; choose them for your dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Preprocess the Seurat object.
set.seed(1)
seu <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = assay(sce_filtered_emptydrops, "counts"))
seu <- NormalizeData(seu)
seu <- FindVariableFeatures(seu, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000)
seu <- ScaleData(seu)
seu <- RunPCA(seu)
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, dims = 1:10)
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Compare neighbourhood sizes without known doublet labels.
set.seed(1)
sweep_messages <- capture.output(
    sweep.res.list <- paramSweep(seu, PCs = 1:10, sct = FALSE)
)
sweep.stats <- summarizeSweep(sweep.res.list, GT = FALSE)
bcmvn <- find.pK(sweep.stats)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(bcmvn, aes(as.numeric(as.character(pK)), BCmetric)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = "pK", y = "BC metric") +
    cowplot::theme_cowplot()
```

```{r}
set.seed(1)
quick_clusters <- scran::quickCluster(
    x = LayerData(object = seu, layer = "data")[VariableFeatures(seu), ]
)
table(quick_clusters)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Estimate the proportion of doublets formed by similar cells (homotypic doublets).
homotypic.prop <- modelHomotypic(quick_clusters)
doublet_rate <- 0.01 # Example: 1%; replace with a rate appropriate for the experiment.
nExp_poi <- round(doublet_rate * ncol(seu))
nExp_poi.adj <- round(nExp_poi * (1 - homotypic.prop))
```

```{r, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# Use the unadjusted expected doublet count.
set.seed(1)
pK <- 0.26 # Example: choose using the pK sweep above.
seu <- doubletFinder(
    seu, PCs = 1:10, pN = 0.25, pK = pK, nExp = nExp_poi,
    reuse.pANN = NULL, sct = FALSE
)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Find output columns without assuming a dataset-specific expected count.
pann_column <- tail(grep("^pANN_", colnames(seu[[]]), value = TRUE), 1)
classification_column <- tail(grep("^DF.classifications_", colnames(seu[[]]), value = TRUE), 1)
seu$doubletfinder_unadjusted <- seu[[classification_column, drop = TRUE]]
table(seu$doubletfinder_unadjusted)
```

```{r, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# Reuse the pANN scores with the homotypic-adjusted expected count.
seu <- doubletFinder(
    seu, PCs = 1:10, pN = 0.25, pK = pK, nExp = nExp_poi.adj,
    reuse.pANN = pann_column, sct = FALSE
)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
adjusted_column <- paste("DF.classifications", 0.25, pK, nExp_poi.adj, sep = "_")
seu$doubletfinder_adjusted <- seu[[adjusted_column, drop = TRUE]]
table(seu$doubletfinder_adjusted)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
doublets_table <- data.frame(
    row.names = colnames(sce_filtered_emptydrops),
    scDblFinder = factor(sce_scdblfinder$scDblFinder.class, c("singlet", "doublet")),
    DoubletFinder = factor(seu$doubletfinder_unadjusted, c("Singlet", "Doublet"))
)
table(doublets_table)
```

# Ambient RNA

Ambient RNA is RNA released into the cell suspension that can be captured
alongside RNA from intact cells. Continue with `sce_filtered_scdblfinder`, after
cell calling and doublet removal.

See the [DecontX tutorial](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/celda/inst/doc/decontX.html)
for details of the method and plots.

- Run `celda::decontX()` to estimate contamination and obtain corrected counts.
  The original `"counts"` assay is retained; corrected counts are stored in
  `"decontXcounts"`.

**Hint:** Use `set.seed()` to make randomised steps reproducible.

```{r, message=FALSE}
set.seed(1)
sce_decontX <- celda::decontX(   )
```

- Plot the clusters on the UMAP layout created by `decontX` with
  `plotDimReduceCluster()`. UMAP provides a two-dimensional view of cell similarities.

**Hint:** Pass cluster labels to `x` and UMAP coordinates to `dim1` and `dim2`.

```{r}
umap <- reducedDim(sce_decontX,    )
plotDimReduceCluster(
    x =   , dim1 =    , dim2 =    
)
```

- Visualise the estimated contamination fraction in each cell.
  Use the `plotDecontXContamination()` function.

```{r}
plotDecontXContamination(   )
```

**Does any cluster display higher (estimated) levels of ambient RNA?**

> Answer:
>
> In the original example, cluster 5 had high estimated contamination, close to
> 1 (100%). Check your plot: cluster numbers and estimates can change between runs.
> High estimates indicate substantial inferred contamination, not a direct measurement.

- Visualise the log-normalised expression of marker genes on a UMAP layout faceted by gene; use `plotDimReduceFeature()`.

**Hint:**

- Use `logNormCounts()` to log-normalise the original counts for plotting.
- `uniquifyFeatureNames()` uses gene symbols where possible, adding identifiers
  to duplicated symbols to keep row names unique. Missing symbols use identifiers.
- Pass a matrix of log-normalised counts and the UMAP coordinates to
  `plotDimReduceFeature()`. Use `exactMatch = TRUE` for exact feature names.

These example markers indicate T cells (`CD3D`, `CD3E`), B cells (`CD79A`,
`CD79B`, `MS4A1`), myeloid cells (`LYZ`, `S100A8`, `S100A9`), and NK or cytotoxic
cells (`GNLY`). Interpret combinations of markers rather than a single gene.

```{r}
sce_decontX <- logNormCounts(sce_decontX, assay.type = "counts")
rownames(sce_decontX) <- uniquifyFeatureNames(
    ID = rownames(sce_decontX),
    names = rowData(sce_decontX)[["Symbol"]]
)
plotDimReduceFeature(
    as.matrix(logcounts(sce_decontX)),
    dim1 = umap[, 1],
    dim2 = umap[, 2],
    features = c(
        "CD3D", "CD3E", "GNLY", "LYZ", "S100A8", "S100A9",
        "CD79A", "CD79B", "MS4A1"
    ),
    exactMatch = TRUE
)
```

- Visualise the percentage of cells with detectable expression of marker genes before and after decontamination as a bar plot; use `plotDecontXMarkerPercentage()`.

**Hint:**

- Create a list of markers grouped by cell type and a list mapping cell types to
  clusters. Pass them to `markers` and `groupClusters`.
- Compare `"counts"`, `"decontXcounts"`, or both with `assayName`.

**Note:** The cluster-to-cell-type mapping below is specific to the original
example. Check marker expression and update the mapping for your results.

```{r}
markers <- list(
    Tcell_Markers = c("CD3E", "CD3D"),
    Bcell_Markers = c("CD79A", "CD79B", "MS4A1"),
    Monocyte_Markers = c("S100A8", "S100A9", "LYZ"),
    NKcell_Markers = "GNLY"
)
# you may wish to change the following {cell type <-> cluster} mappings
cellTypeMappings <- list(
    Bcells = 4,
    Monocytes = 2,
    Tcells = c(1, 3),
    NKcells = c(5, 6)
)
plotDecontXMarkerPercentage(
    sce_decontX,
    markers = markers,
    groupClusters = cellTypeMappings,
    assayName = "counts"
)
```

```{r}
plotDecontXMarkerPercentage(
    sce_decontX,
    markers = markers,
    groupClusters = cellTypeMappings,
    assayName = "decontXcounts" # <- notice the change here
)
```

```{r}
plotDecontXMarkerPercentage(
    sce_decontX,
    markers = markers,
    groupClusters = cellTypeMappings,
    assayName = c("counts", "decontXcounts") # <- notice the change here
)
```

- Compare original and decontaminated marker counts with violin plots using
  `plotDecontXMarkerExpression()`. These plots use counts by default, rather than
  the `"logcounts"` assay created earlier.

**Hint:**

- Each marker and cell type produces a panel. Use markers from one cell type
  to keep the figure readable, for example `markers[["Monocyte_Markers"]]`.
- Pass the cluster-to-cell-type mapping to `groupClusters`.

```{r}
plotDecontXMarkerExpression(
    sce_decontX,
    markers =    ,
    groupClusters =   ,
    ncol = 
)
```
